lessons.title: Courage Is a Skill, Not a Trait
lessons.key_idea: Brave leadership comes from teachable, observable skills, so anyone who develops people and processes can learn to lead with courage.

lessons.title: Vulnerability Is Not Weakness
lessons.key_idea: Vulnerability is the uncertainty, risk and emotional exposure behind every act of courage, and the common myths about it, such as that it is weakness or oversharing, keep leaders stuck.

lessons.title: Take Off the Armor
lessons.key_idea: Leaders often protect themselves with armor like perfectionism, cynicism and needing to be the knower, and swapping it for daring behaviors is what unlocks trust and innovation.

lessons.title: Clear Is Kind
lessons.key_idea: Avoiding hard conversations or being vague to spare feelings is actually unkind, while honest, clear expectations and feedback are a form of respect.

lessons.title: Live Into Two Core Values
lessons.key_idea: Narrowing your values to two and defining the specific behaviors that show them gives you a guide for decisions when things get hard.

lessons.title: Braving Trust, Behavior by Behavior
lessons.key_idea: Trust becomes something teams can talk about and build when it is broken into seven concrete behaviors: boundaries, reliability, accountability, the vault, integrity, non-judgment and generosity.

lessons.title: Learning to Rise After Falling
lessons.key_idea: Daring leaders recover from setbacks by noticing their emotions, questioning the story they are telling themselves, and turning what they learn into braver action, which ties every skill together.

plan.title: Dare to Lead
plan.author: Brené Brown
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's structure and core concepts well, including its four skill sets, the vulnerability myths, the BRAVING trust model, and the Learning to Rise process.
plan.one_liner: Courage isn't a personality trait. It's a set of teachable skills, and every leader can learn them.
plan.summary: Brené Brown draws on her research into courage, shame and vulnerability to argue that brave leadership is built from learnable skills, not innate charisma. She defines a leader as anyone who takes responsibility for finding the potential in people and processes and has the courage to develop it. The book is organised around four skill sets. The first is rumbling with vulnerability, which means staying in hard conversations instead of armoring up. The second is living into a small number of clearly defined values. The third is braving trust, which breaks trust into specific behaviors people can discuss. The fourth is learning to rise after failure. Along the way Brown dismantles myths about vulnerability, shows why clarity is a form of kindness, and explains how armored leadership quietly kills innovation, trust and belonging.
